summary: A first-person account of the city's transit strike that began on September 20, 2023, describing how stalled buses and trains have stranded commuters and disrupted daily life. It profiles affected residents, makeshift alternatives like bikes, shuttles and taxis, and the toll on local businesses. The author closes by describing a city waiting uncertainly for a resolution to the labor dispute.
one_line: A commuter's first-person report on the September 20, 2023 transit strike and its effects on residents, businesses, and alternative transportation.
key_facts: The transit strike began on September 20, 2023, after negotiations between the city's transportation department and transit worker unions reached an impasse.
The strike was announced the evening before by the major transit unions and is described as the largest labor disruption the city has seen in decades.
Jennifer Miles, an operator with over 15 years on the job, became a de facto spokesperson for the strike movement.
Abigail Torres, a mother of two who relies on buses, has to wake up two hours earlier to get her kids to school on time.
The city is offering shuttles, encouraging carpooling, and trying to negotiate with ride-share companies, which the author calls a band-aid solution.
Frank Donovan offers bike rental services at an affordable rate to stranded commuters.
City bike lanes have become as congested as the roads, but cycling is not an option for people with disabilities or long highway-dependent commutes.
Taxis remain the only reliable but costly option for many, with lengthening queues.
Marcus Li, a coffee shop owner, reports a plummet in morning sales, saying 'We operate on thin margins; this could sink us.'
Michael Chen, a caregiver, struggles to reach his elderly clients who depend on his aid.
Lila Rodriguez, a high school senior, is missing college prep course sessions for her SATs because of the strike.
The strike is driven by a battle for fair wages and improved work conditions.
